title: Git Blame and Annotate
description: Use git blame to trace the history of each line and find who changed what and when.

data.text: git blame shows the author, commit, and timestamp for every line in a file. It is the primary tool for understanding why a specific line of code exists, who introduced it, and what commit message explains it. Use it alongside bisect for powerful debugging workflows.
git blame <file> displays each line with its last-modifying commit hash, author, timestamp, and line number. This tells you exactly who last touched each line and in what context.

data.title: Run git blame on a file
data.code:
# Basic blame
git blame src/auth/LoginService.cs

# Ignore whitespace changes
git blame -w src/auth/LoginService.cs

# Show only lines that match a pattern
git blame -L 50,80 src/auth/LoginService.cs

# Show the original commit even after line was moved/copied
git blame -C src/auth/LoginService.cs

# Show the commit message for each line
git blame --show-name --show-number --show-email src/auth/LoginService.cs

data.text: Use the -C flag to detect lines that were copied or moved from another file. This is useful when a function was extracted or inlined and you need to find its original location.

data.title: Trace moved code with -C
data.code:
# Detect moved/copied code across files
git blame -C -C src/auth/LoginService.cs

# Show original location for copied lines

# Detect lines moved within the same file
git blame -M src/auth/LoginService.cs

data.title: Pair blame with the commit message
data.text: After identifying the commit with blame, view it with git show <sha> to see the full context: the commit message, diff, and any related changes. This often reveals the 'why' behind the code.

items: **Why is this line here?** — git blame to find the commit, git show to read the message
**Who can review this change?** — blame shows the author, who is the best person to explain it
**When was this introduced?** — blame timestamp tells you when the line was added
**Find the original source** — blame -C to trace code across files

data.text: git annotate is an alias for git blame with identical functionality. Some Git GUIs use annotate in their UI. Both commands accept the same flags and produce the same output.

data.title: Git annotate is equivalent to blame
data.code:
# These are identical:
git blame src/auth/LoginService.cs
git annotate src/auth/LoginService.cs

# Same flags work:
git annotate -L 1,50 -w src/auth/LoginService.cs

data.text: Both GitHub and GitLab provide a blame view in their web UIs. Click the blame button on any file to see line-by-line attribution with clickable commit links. This is more accessible than the command-line version for non-technical reviewers.

data.title: Blame a specific version of a file
data.code:
# Blame a file at a specific tag or commit
git blame v2.1.0 -- src/auth/LoginService.cs

# Blame the version from 6 months ago
git blame --date=relative --since="6 months ago" src/auth/LoginService.cs

# Blame only the first commit that touched a line
git blame --first-parent src/auth/LoginService.cs

items.question: Does git blame show the first or last modification?
items.answer: git blame shows the last commit that modified each line. Use git blame --first-parent to see only commits on the first-parent chain.

items.question: Can blame trace across merge commits?
items.answer: By default, blame follows the commit graph. Use -C to detect lines that were moved across files, including during merges.

items.question: Is git blame accurate for large refactors?
items.answer: Yes, but large refactors may show the refactor commit as the author of many lines. Use -C to find the original source of the code before the refactor.

items.question: Does blame work on deleted files?
items.answer: Yes. Use git blame <commit> -- <path> where <commit> is a commit when the file existed, and <path> is the path to the deleted file.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: git blame shows author, commit, and timestamp for every line
Use -C to detect moved/copied code across files
Pair blame with git show <sha> to read the commit message
Blame a specific version with git blame <tag> -- <file>
GitHub and GitLab provide web-based blame views for easier review
